claims.claim: Preference evidence and task-specific authorization are behaviorally distinct intervention signals in the controlled protocol.
Masking or shuffling authorization evidence sharply increases error and unauthorized autonomous action in the text baseline.
Canonical-set performance overstates generalization under held-out permission and preference paraphrases.
Repeated-trial consistency can be substantially lower than single-trial pass rate under seeded action noise.
A state-tracking authorization policy handles delayed confirmation and transient environment failures that break a static rule policy.
Failed trajectories can be deterministically mined into prioritized incidents and weighted preference-training records.
Holding preference evidence fixed while authorization changes exposes stale-authority, premature-execution, repeated-ask, and update-latency failures that are hidden by static permission evaluation.
An authorization label is insufficient when a grant is bound to an obsolete action scope; scope/version provenance exposes stale-grant execution hidden by the simpler transition suite.
Authorization validity depends on grant provenance; replay, wrong-principal, cross-request, resource, revision, and delegated-authority mismatches expose failures hidden by a latest-label policy.

Authorization must remain valid across scope, expiry, replay history, principal identity, concurrent requests, and delegation ancestry; flat provenance checks are insufficient under composed authority changes.

Each targeted capability-validity invariant is independently exercised: deleting expiry, nonce, parent-delegation, request, principal, resource, or revision checks causes measurable benchmark failure.
